name: Proximal (long head) biceps rupture
aka: ruptured biceps tendon at the shoulder
populations: people with rotator cuff tendinopathy or tears
manual workers who lift heavy loads
summary: Rupture of the long head of biceps at the shoulder, usually in an older or tendinopathic tendon, with a pop, bruising and a 'Popeye' bulge. Most people do well without surgery, with a modest loss of strength.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Pain and bruising settle over weeks (clinical convention); the muscle bulge is permanent without surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; commonly about 3 months after non-operative care once pain and strength allow, longer after tenodesis (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Inspection for a Popeye deformity with resisted elbow flexion, plus a cuff examination; Speed's and Yergason's tests add little

keyFacts.label: Strength loss without surgery
keyFacts.value: In a small old isokinetic series, elbow flexion fell by 16% and supination by 11% (10 patients); a review quotes 8–21%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound is highly specific for complete rupture (LR+ 35.50); MRI specificity is 93.0%–99.0%

keyFacts.label: Proportion proximal
keyFacts.value: About 3% of all biceps tendon ruptures are distal, so most are proximal

overview:
Proximal biceps rupture is almost always a rupture of the long head tendon. Most biceps tendon ruptures are proximal: only about 3% occur at the distal insertion [r1]. The tendon usually fails in a hypovascular, degenerated segment, and the rupture often coexists with rotator cuff pathology [r2]. Degenerative change in the long head is the usual cause [r3], and biceps and cuff tendon changes accumulate together with age [r4]. The person typically feels a pop or sudden sharp pain, often during a modest lifting task, and then notices bruising and a bulge in the lower arm (the 'Popeye' deformity) as the muscle belly slides distally.

What is lost is modest. In a small old study with isokinetic testing (10 patients treated conservatively, 5 surgically, and 20 healthy controls), the conservative group lost 16% of elbow flexion strength and 11% of forearm supination strength, compared with 8% and 7% in the surgical group [r5]. A review quotes a loss of only 8–21% of elbow flexion and supination power without surgery, and describes good results with non-operative treatment [r3]. These are small, non-randomised, decades-old data, and the strength figures should be treated as approximate. The reason that many people do well without surgery is that the distal biceps insertion and the short head remain intact and brachialis still flexes the elbow (anatomical reasoning). Residual pain after rupture is often from associated subacromial or cuff problems rather than the rupture itself [r3].

The indication for repair is a matter of patient priorities rather than trial evidence. Surgery has been recommended for younger people, manual workers and sportspeople, and rarely for cosmetic reasons or for impingement from a disturbing tendon stump [r5]. Refixation was described as offering a small but evident gain in flexion and supination power and a way to correct the deformity [r3]. The trials that compare tenotomy with tenodesis were done in people with painful, mostly intact long head tendon lesions, not in completed ruptures, so they are indirect evidence: in one double-blind trial the cosmetic deformity rate was 33% after tenotomy and 10% after tenodesis, with no difference in pain, function or strength [r6]. No randomised trial of repair versus non-operative care after an acute proximal rupture was found in the sources reviewed here.

epidemiology.text: The sources reviewed here did not give a population incidence rate for proximal biceps rupture. About 3% of all biceps tendon ruptures occur at the distal insertion, so most are proximal [r1], and the long head is the usual site [r3]. Proximal ruptures typically occur in hypovascular, degenerative tendon and often coexist with rotator cuff pathology [r2]. In 406 MRIs obtained for shoulder pain, long head tendinopathy became more common with each year of age (odds ratio 1.04) and was strongly associated with cuff pathology (odds ratio 6.9), and everyone aged 85 or over had both [r4]. Those data describe tendinopathy rather than rupture, but they fit the picture of an age-related tendon that is already abnormal before it ruptures. Rarely, rupture follows attrition of the tendon over a malunited proximal humerus fracture: a case report described a long head rupture with the proximal stump displaced inside the joint [r7].

intrinsic: Age over about 40 years and degenerative tendon change [r3,r4]
Pre-existing long head tendinopathy, often with anterior shoulder pain before the rupture [r2,r4]
Rotator cuff tendinopathy or tear, which commonly coexists [r2,r4]
A hypovascular tendon segment, in which rupture usually occurs [r2]
extrinsic: A sudden heavy lift or an unexpected load on the flexed arm (clinical observation)
Heavy manual work and repetitive lifting (clinical observation)
Repetitive overhead activity that loads the tendon in the groove (clinical observation)

mechanism.summary: The tendon usually fails in an older or already degenerate segment under a load that would not injure a healthy tendon: typically a sudden forceful contraction or an unexpected pull while the biceps is working eccentrically, such as lifting or catching a heavy object (clinical observation) [r2,r3]. The rupture usually occurs inside the joint close to its origin at the labrum [r7], and the muscle then retracts toward the elbow, producing the Popeye bulge.
sequence: A degenerate, hypovascular long head tendon, often already painful from tendinopathy, is loaded in everyday lifting [r2,r4].
A sudden heavy load or an unexpected pull stretches the contracting biceps (eccentric overload) while the elbow is flexed and the arm is in front of the body.
The weakened tendon fibres fail and the tendon ruptures, usually completely, with a pop or sharp pain.
The loose proximal stump retracts, and the muscle belly slides toward the elbow because its distal insertion and short head remain intact.
The muscle bunches in the lower arm (Popeye deformity), bruising tracks down the arm, and pain often falls within days to weeks.
The biceps still works through the short head and the distal insertion, so flexion and supination weaken modestly rather than fail [r3,r5].

variants.name: Degenerative rupture of the long head (typical)
variants.description: Older adult, often with tendinopathy or cuff disease, minimal trauma [r2,r3,r4].

variants.name: Rupture associated with a rotator cuff tear
variants.description: Cuff pathology coexists in many people; residual shoulder pain after rupture often comes from the cuff or subacromial space [r2,r3].

variants.name: Traumatic rupture in a younger person
variants.description: Uncommon; younger people, manual workers and athletes are the group in whom surgery has been recommended [r5].

variants.name: Partial tear that progresses to rupture
variants.description: Prodromal anterior shoulder pain from tendinopathy is common before a complete rupture (clinical observation); see long head of biceps tendinopathy.

variants.name: Rupture with the stump displaced into the joint
variants.description: A rare case of a retracted proximal stump caused locking and internal impingement; tenotomy with stump removal gave relief [r7].

anatomy.text: The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum, crosses the humeral head within the joint, and exits through the rotator interval into the bicipital groove, where the transverse humeral ligament and the sheath hold it in place. It joins the short head, which arises from the coracoid, in the biceps muscle belly. The distal tendon inserts on the radial tuberosity and flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm. After a proximal rupture of the long head, the short head and the distal insertion remain in continuity, brachialis continues to flex the elbow, and the supinator contributes to supination, which is why strength loss is modest. The pectoralis major tendon inserts just lateral to the groove, which is relevant when palpating after bruising.

structures.name: Long head of biceps tendon
structures.role: Intra-articular and groove segment; the usual site of proximal rupture, most often inside the joint near the labrum [r3,r7]

structures.name: Short head of biceps and coracoid origin
structures.role: Remains attached, so the muscle still works after long head rupture (anatomical reasoning)

structures.name: Bicipital groove, transverse humeral ligament and sheath
structures.role: Hold the tendon in the groove; the retracted tendon end may lie in the joint or the groove (anatomical reasoning)

structures.name: Biceps brachii muscle belly
structures.role: Elbow flexion and forearm supination; bunches distally after rupture (Popeye deformity)

structures.name: Distal biceps tendon at the radial tuberosity
structures.role: Remains intact; its rupture is a separate injury with much greater loss of supination and flexion [r3]

structures.name: Rotator cuff tendons
structures.role: Often coexistent pathology that determines residual shoulder pain and function [r2,r3]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In proximal biceps rupture the tendon usually fails in tissue that was already abnormal. Proximal ruptures occur in hypovascular, degenerative tendon and often coexist with cuff pathology [r2], and degenerative change within the tendon is the usual cause [r3]. Tendon changes in the biceps and the cuff accumulate together with age [r4], so a force that would not injure a healthy tendon can complete a tear in a degenerate one. After rupture the proximal stump retracts, and because the tendon lies inside a synovial joint, the stumps are bathed in synovial fluid and bridging healing across the gap is not expected (conceptual model; the stump seldom reattaches).

The muscle remains in continuity through its short head and its distal insertion, and the arm keeps most of its function. A small old isokinetic study found elbow flexion strength down by 16% and supination down by 11% without surgery, and shoulder abduction strength down by 16% [r5]. The deformity and the cramping that some people notice reflect the retracted muscle belly rather than a loss of the whole muscle. Because many ruptured tendons were already painful and abnormal, some people find the shoulder more comfortable after the rupture than before it (clinical observation, not measured in the sources reviewed).

structures.name: Long head of biceps tendon
structures.effect: Complete rupture, usually inside the joint close to the labral origin; the proximal stump retracts [r7]

structures.name: Tendon sheath and bicipital groove
structures.effect: Haemorrhage and bruising track distally; sheath irritation is common before rupture [r4]

structures.name: Rotator cuff tendons
structures.effect: Concomitant tendinopathy or tear in many people; may be the source of residual pain [r2,r3]

structures.name: Superior labrum and glenohumeral joint
structures.effect: The stump may lie in the joint and in rare cases cause locking or impingement [r7]

structures.name: Subacromial space
structures.effect: Residual complaints after conservative treatment often result from associated subacromial problems [r3]

muscles.name: Biceps brachii
muscles.effect: Muscle belly retracts and bunches distally (Popeye deformity); loses some elbow flexion and supination strength [r5]

muscles.name: Rotator cuff and deltoid
muscles.effect: May be weak from pre-existing tendinopathy or tear; shoulder abduction strength was also reduced in the isokinetic study [r5]

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers
muscles.effect: Altered recruitment with pain and with the changed arm lever (clinical observation)

cellular.description: Blood from the torn tendon and muscle tracks down the arm as bruising; neutrophils and macrophages clear debris.

cellular.phase: Proliferation of the stump and sheath
cellular.description: Fibroblasts and new capillaries form disorganised collagen at the tendon end; the proximal stump retracts and does not bridge the gap in the joint (conceptual model).
The muscle adapts to its new length and the stump forms scar tissue in the groove or joint; the deformity persists without surgery.

The tendon is fixed to the humerus and healing takes weeks to become secure, which is why surgeons restrict early resisted elbow flexion. MRI at one year showed intact tenodesis in all patients of one trial [r6].

systems.effect: Acute nociceptive pain at the time of rupture; pain often falls afterwards (clinical observation). Persistent pain should lead to examination of the cuff and subacromial space [r3]
Bruising down the arm to the elbow in the first week or two; very large or expanding haematoma is unusual and warrants medical review
Cuff, scapular and trunk control affect residual shoulder function; the cuff is often co-affected [r2,r4]
Biceps tendinopathy and cuff tendinopathy rise together with age [r4], so rupture is an end point of an age-related tendon process in most people
Concern about the visible deformity and what it means for the arm; reassurance about modest functional loss is often important [r3,r5]

timeframes.summary: No trial in the sources reviewed here described the recovery time course after proximal biceps rupture, so the phases below are clinical conventions. Pain and bruising settle quickly compared with most tendon injuries, and function is limited by cuff status rather than by the rupture [r3].

healing.description: Analgesia, early gentle movement and reassurance. Bruising tracks down the arm (clinical convention).
Full pain-free range of shoulder and elbow and light loading of biceps and cuff. After tenodesis, follow the surgeon's restrictions on resisted elbow flexion.
Progressive strengthening of elbow flexion, supination, cuff and scapular muscles, then return to heavy tasks and sport.

milestones.label: Resisted elbow flexion begins after tenodesis
milestones.note: Common clinical convention; follow the surgeon's protocol

milestones.label: Strength testing against the other side
milestones.note: Expect a modest deficit without surgery [r3,r5]

milestones.label: Return to heavy lifting or sport
milestones.note: Criteria-based; longer after tenodesis or with cuff pathology

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. After non-operative care, commonly about 3 months, once pain, range and strength allow (clinical convention). After tenodesis, the timeline follows the surgeon's protocol and any concomitant cuff repair. The sources reviewed here did not give standard return-to-sport times.

symptoms: A sudden pop or sharp pain in the front of the shoulder or upper arm, often during a lifting task
Bruising tracking down the upper arm and sometimes to the elbow
A bulge in the lower upper arm, noticed within hours to days
Aching or cramping in the biceps with sustained or repeated elbow flexion
Mild weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination
Often prodromal anterior shoulder pain before the rupture, which may settle afterwards [r4]
signs: Popeye deformity: the biceps belly bunches distally, most obvious with resisted elbow flexion
Ecchymosis over the anterior arm and sometimes the antecubital fossa
Tenderness or an empty bicipital groove
Near-normal elbow flexion strength, with mild weakness in supination and flexion compared with the other side [r5]
Cuff signs (painful arc, weakness, lag signs) in some people with coexistent cuff pathology [r4]
Normal distal biceps tendon at the elbow (hook test normal)

subjective: Mechanism: a sudden heavy lift or pull with a pop, or a gradual onset with later deformity
Prior anterior shoulder pain, previous cuff problems, injections or surgery
Hand dominance, occupation, sport and cosmetic concerns
Pain pattern now: location, night pain, and pain with overhead reach
Cramping with elbow flexion and any weakness in supination or lifting
Age, general health, medicines (including anticoagulants, which worsen bruising) and red-flag screen
observation: Biceps contour at rest and with resisted elbow flexion, compared with the other side: look for the Popeye deformity
Bruising on the upper arm, chest wall or antecubital fossa
Muscle bulk of biceps, cuff fossae and deltoid
palpation: Bicipital groove (tender or empty) with the arm in slight internal rotation
Biceps muscle belly and the myotendinous region
Distal biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa to exclude distal rupture
Greater tuberosity, AC joint and the pectoralis major insertion
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive shoulder elevation, rotation and hand-behind-back
Elbow flexion and extension, and forearm pronation and supination
Cervical spine range to screen neck contribution
strength: Resisted elbow flexion with the forearm supinated, pronated and neutral, compared with the other side [r5]
Resisted forearm supination with the elbow flexed to 90°
Resisted external rotation, abduction and internal rotation for the cuff, with lag signs [r4]
Hand-held dynamometry for objective strength and limb symmetry
neuro: Upper limb neurological screen: myotomes, dermatomes and reflexes
Musculocutaneous nerve sensation (lateral forearm) and function if weakness is out of proportion to the rupture
Cervical screen if neck pain or neurological symptoms are present
functional: Gym tasks such as curls, pull-ups and rows
Patient concern about appearance and cramping

specialTests.name: Inspection for Popeye deformity with resisted elbow flexion
specialTests.purpose: To confirm retraction of the biceps muscle belly after long head rupture
specialTests.procedure: With the elbow flexed to 90° and the forearm supinated, ask the patient to flex against resistance and compare the muscle contour with the other side.
specialTests.positive: The muscle bulges distally with a loss of contour in the proximal arm. Accuracy figures were not found in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Ludington's test
specialTests.purpose: To check for continuity of the long head tendon
specialTests.procedure: With the hands clasped on top of the head, ask the patient to contract both biceps isometrically while the examiner palpates the groove region on each side.
specialTests.positive: No tendon is felt tensing in the groove on the affected side. Accuracy figures were not found in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Speed's and Yergason's tests
specialTests.purpose: Not useful for confirming rupture; they test for painful biceps pathology and are insensitive
specialTests.procedure: See long head of biceps tendinopathy for the procedures.
specialTests.positive: In the long head tendinopathy literature, test accuracy was poor and a systematic review recommended no individual special test [r9]; they add little once a Popeye deformity is visible.

specialTests.name: Hook test and biceps squeeze test (distal biceps)
specialTests.purpose: To exclude a distal biceps rupture, which has much greater consequences
specialTests.procedure: Hook test: the examiner attempts to hook an index finger under the lateral edge of the distal biceps tendon at the elbow with the elbow flexed and the forearm supinated. Squeeze test: squeeze the biceps belly and watch for forearm supination.
specialTests.positive: An absent hook, or no supination on squeeze, suggests distal rupture. The review describes both as specific for distal rupture and gave no figures [r1].

clinicalRules.name: Exclude distal biceps rupture
clinicalRules.description: Distal ruptures are a different injury: about 3% of biceps ruptures [r1], with a non-operative loss of 30–40% of flexion power and over 50% of supination power, and they should generally be treated operatively [r3]. Check the antecubital fossa, bruising and supination strength.

clinicalRules.name: Always examine the cuff
clinicalRules.description: Residual complaints after conservative treatment often result from associated subacromial problems [r3], and the difficulty lies in separating isolated biceps pathology from a concomitant cuff tear or instability [r8]. Test cuff strength and lag signs, and image if weakness is more than expected.

clinicalRules.name: Strength figures are approximate
clinicalRules.description: The figures for strength loss come from a ten-patient conservative group tested in the 1980s [r5] and a narrative review [r3]; individual deficits vary, and none of the sources reviewed here measured loss after acute rupture with modern tools.

outcomeMeasures.name: Constant–Murley score or SPADI
outcomeMeasures.use: Shoulder function and the effect of cuff pathology

outcomeMeasures.name: QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Arm function and work or sport demands

outcomeMeasures.name: Hand-held dynamometry or isokinetic testing of elbow flexion and supination
outcomeMeasures.use: Strength deficit and limb symmetry, as in the isokinetic study [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating scale (0–10)
outcomeMeasures.use: Shoulder pain, cramping and night pain

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-reported satisfaction with appearance
outcomeMeasures.use: Cosmetic concern, a main reason for repair [r3,r6]

imaging.indication: When the diagnosis is unclear, there is no Popeye deformity, or the cuff needs checking
imaging.findings: Highly specific for complete rupture: pooled LR+ 35.50 and LR− 0.30 [r9]. Also assesses the cuff.

imaging.indication: Suspected cuff tear, planning surgery, or an unclear picture
imaging.findings: Specificity 93.0%–99.0% for complete tears, with more variable sensitivity (55.9%–90.0%) and an overall LR+ of 37.3 and LR− of 0.29 [r10]

imaging.indication: After a fall or trauma, or to exclude fracture, calcification and arthritis
imaging.findings: No tendon information; may show humeral head position or calcific deposit (clinical convention)

differentials.name: Distal biceps rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Antecubital pain and bruising, a missing distal tendon (hook test), proximal retraction of the muscle and marked supination weakness [r1,r3].

differentials.name: Long head of biceps tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Groove pain with loading but a normal muscle contour; no pop or Popeye deformity.

differentials.name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: Weakness of elevation or external rotation with lag signs after a fall or pull; the cuff and biceps may be torn together.

differentials.name: Pectoralis major rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Chest and axillary bruising with loss of the axillary fold, after a forceful bench press or grappling event.

differentials.name: SLAP lesion
differentials.distinguishing: Deep pain with overhead activity and clicking, without a Popeye deformity.

differentials.name: Degenerative rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual weakness and pain without a sudden pop in the arm; may coexist with biceps rupture [r4].

differentials.name: Proximal humerus fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness, crepitus and extensive bruising after a fall; confirmed on radiograph.

differentials.name: Muscle strain or haematoma of the biceps
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and bruising in the muscle belly after a strain, with intact tendon continuity and no Popeye deformity.

redFlags: Antecubital pain, bruising and supination weakness with a proximally retracted biceps muscle: possible distal biceps rupture, which should be assessed by an orthopaedic surgeon promptly because early anatomical reattachment is the goal [r1,r3].
Weakness of elevation or external rotation that is more than pain-limited, or a lag sign: possible associated cuff tear. Arrange ultrasound or MRI and an orthopaedic opinion [r8].
Expanding swelling, tense arm, severe pain out of proportion, or a cold, pale or numb hand: possible significant haematoma, vascular or neurological injury. Emergency assessment.
Chest pain, breathlessness, sweating or pain spreading to the jaw with shoulder or arm pain: possible cardiac cause. Emergency assessment.
Fever, a hot red swollen arm or wound drainage after surgery: possible infection. Same-day medical review.
After tenodesis: sudden loss of the repair with a new Popeye deformity or a 'pop' during rehabilitation. Contact the surgeon and stop resisted loading until reviewed.
Persistent locking, catching or deep shoulder pain after rupture: a retracted stump in the joint can rarely impinge. Refer for imaging and orthopaedic review [r7].

management.principles: Most people with a proximal biceps rupture can be managed non-operatively. The loss is modest (a conservative group lost 16% of elbow flexion and 11% of supination strength in one small study, and a review quotes 8–21%) [r5,r3], and in clinical experience many people find the shoulder more comfortable once the painful tendon has ruptured. The decision about surgery is a shared one, based on age, occupation, sport, concern about appearance and cramping, and cuff status. Surgery (tenodesis) has been recommended for younger people, manual workers and sportspeople, rarely for cosmetic reasons, and for impingement from a tendon stump [r5], and it offers a small but evident gain in flexion and supination power with correction of the deformity [r3]. There is no randomised comparison of repair versus non-operative care after acute rupture. The nearest evidence compares tenotomy with tenodesis in intact painful tendons and shows similar pain and function with a Popeye deformity more frequent after tenotomy [r11,r6,r12]. The most important physiotherapy task is to examine the cuff and subacromial space, because that is where persistent symptoms usually originate [r3].

medical.name: Non-operative management with analgesia and early movement
medical.description: Short-term simple analgesia, early gentle movement and a return to light tasks, with reassurance about the modest loss of strength and the permanent bulge. In a small old study the conservative group lost 16% of elbow flexion and 11% of supination strength, compared with 8% and 7% after surgery [r5]. A review describes good non-operative results with a loss of 8–21% of flexion and supination power [r3], and a case report notes that treatment of long head rupture is usually non-operative with good outcomes [r7]. These are small, non-randomised data.

medical.name: Ultrasound or MRI when the picture is unclear or the cuff may be torn
medical.description: Ultrasound is highly specific for complete rupture (LR+ 35.50, LR− 0.30) [r9], and MRI specificity is 93.0%–99.0% with variable sensitivity [r10]. Imaging is most useful to check the cuff and to confirm rupture when there is no Popeye deformity or the diagnosis is uncertain, not to confirm a visible rupture.

medical.name: Tenodesis (repair) for selected patients
medical.description: Considered for younger people, manual workers, sportspeople and those troubled by the deformity, or by impingement from a stump [r5]; a review described refixation as offering a small but evident gain in flexion and supination power and effective correction of the deformity [r3]. Indirect evidence from tenotomy-versus-tenodesis trials in people with painful long head lesions shows no difference in pain or function and a lower Popeye deformity rate with tenodesis: 10% versus 33% at 24 months in a double-blind trial [r6], odds ratio 0.29 in a meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials [r11], and four of seven trials favouring tenodesis for deformity, cramping, satisfaction and/or supination strength in another review [r12]. A meta-analysis found no evidence-based benefit of tenodesis over tenotomy for function, pain or strength, and it remains unclear whether younger people benefit [r13].

medical.name: Treatment of associated cuff or subacromial pathology
medical.description: Residual complaints after conservative treatment often result from associated subacromial problems [r3], and distinguishing isolated biceps pathology from concomitant cuff disease is difficult [r8]. Manage the cuff on its own merits (see the cuff pages) rather than attributing pain to the biceps.

physio.name: Education and reassurance about expected course
physio.description: Explain that function is usually near normal, that pain and bruising settle, that the bulge is cosmetic and persists without surgery, and that surgery is a choice rather than a necessity. The expected strength loss is modest but variable [r5,r3].

physio.name: Progressive shoulder, scapular and elbow strengthening
physio.description: After pain settles, restore range and then progressively load elbow flexion, supination, the cuff and the scapular stabilisers. No randomised trial of rehabilitation after proximal biceps rupture was found in the sources reviewed, so the program is expert opinion.

physio.name: Post-tenodesis rehabilitation to the surgeon's protocol
physio.description: Protect the fixation with a sling and restricted resisted elbow flexion for the period the surgeon specifies (commonly about 4–6 weeks; clinical convention), then progress range, light loading and strengthening. Tenodesis may subject the patient to a longer rehabilitation process than tenotomy [r8].

physio.name: Assuming persistent shoulder pain is from the rupture alone
physio.description: Persistent pain after rupture often comes from the cuff or subacromial space [r3], and it is hard to separate isolated biceps pathology from concomitant cuff disease or instability [r8]. Examine and treat the whole shoulder.

physio.name: Resisted active elbow flexion or heavy lifting in the protected phase after tenodesis
physio.description: Loading the new fixation too early risks failure and recurrent deformity (clinical reasoning). Follow the surgeon's protocol.

education: A ruptured biceps tendon at the shoulder is common in older adults and is usually not serious. The arm keeps most of its strength.
The bulge in the upper arm is caused by the muscle bunching up. It is a cosmetic change and does not usually affect function much.
Pain and bruising settle over a few weeks. Keep moving the arm and return to your tasks gradually.

Surgery to reattach the tendon is an option if the appearance, cramping or strength bothers you, or if you do heavy manual work or sport. It gives only a small improvement in strength and has its own risks and rehabilitation [r5,r3].
If the shoulder stays painful or weak, the rotator cuff may be involved, and that is worth examining and treating.
See a doctor promptly if the pain is at the elbow with weakness turning the palm up, if the arm swells tensely, or if the hand turns cold or numb.

rehab.overview: The program below is for non-operative management and, with modification, after tenodesis. No trial of rehabilitation after proximal biceps rupture was found in the sources reviewed, so the stages and doses are clinical conventions. The priorities are to restore shoulder range, rebuild elbow flexion and supination strength within pain tolerance, and treat any coexisting cuff pathology, since that is the usual cause of residual symptoms [r3]. After tenodesis, the surgeon's restrictions on resisted elbow flexion and lifting take priority.

stages.name: Settle and keep moving
precautions: After tenodesis: sling and no resisted active elbow flexion until cleared
Avoid heavy lifting and sudden loading of the arm
Report increasing swelling, tense arm, numbness or a cold hand

exercises.name: Pendulum swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang and swing from the trunk

exercises.name: Active-assisted shoulder elevation
exercises.cues: Lead with the other hand; stop short of pain

exercises.name: Elbow, wrist and hand range of motion and grip
Scapular setting and posture
exercises.cues: Gently draw the shoulder blades back and down

progressionCriteria: Full elbow range and near-full shoulder range
Surgeon's clearance to start loading if tenodesis was performed

stages.name: Restore range and light loading
goals: Begin light loading of elbow flexors, cuff and scapular stabilisers
precautions: After tenodesis: resisted elbow flexion only when cleared (commonly after about 6 weeks)
Keep pain ≤ 3–4/10 during exercise and settling within 24 hours (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Active elevation in the scapular plane
Wall slide
exercises.cues: Keep the forearms on the wall and the shoulder blade moving

exercises.name: Isometric external rotation at the side
exercises.cues: Elbow bent and tucked, press into a wall

exercises.name: Isometric elbow flexion and supination (non-operative or once cleared)
exercises.cues: Elbow at the side; build gradually over days

progressionCriteria: Full or near-full active elevation without hitching
Isometric elbow flexion tolerated without flare over 24 hours

stages.name: Progressive strengthening
goals: Restore elbow flexion and supination strength
Return to lifting and pulling tasks
precautions: Increase load by about 5–10% per week and monitor pain over the next 24 hours (clinical convention)
Post-tenodesis: heavy loading only with the surgeon's clearance

exercises.name: Slow elbow flexion (curl) with a supinated grip
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12 with 3 s lowering, 2–3 times per week
exercises.cues: Elbow at the side; control the lowering

exercises.name: Row
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades back and down

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–15 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week

exercises.name: Scaption raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Raise in the scapular plane with no shrug

exercises.name: Incline or wall push-up plus
exercises.cues: Push through the hands and protract at the top

progressionCriteria: Strength about 80% or more of the other side for elbow flexion, supination and external rotation
Pain ≤ 2/10 with loaded exercise and daily tasks
No flare over 24 hours after heavier sessions

stages.name: Return to heavy work and sport
goals: Return to heavy lifting, pulling and sport
precautions: Return to heavy and overhead tasks only when criteria are met
Build volume gradually (about 10–20% per week; clinical convention)

exercises.name: Overhead press
exercises.cues: Control the lowering; press in the scapular plane

exercises.name: Farmer or suitcase carry
exercises.cues: Tall posture with the shoulder blades set

exercises.name: Pull-up or heavy row progression
exercises.cues: Start with assisted or eccentric versions; scapulae set

exercises.name: Sport- or work-specific drills (lifting, pulling, throwing)
exercises.dosage: Start at about 25–30% of normal volume and build over 4–8 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality first, then volume, then intensity

progressionCriteria: Passes strength, range and function criteria (see return to sport)
Completes work or sport simulation at full volume with pain ≤ 2/10
Surgeon clearance if tenodesis was performed

criteria: Pain ≤ 2/10 with work or sport tasks and no night pain
Full pain-free active range of motion equal to the other side
Elbow flexion and supination strength about 90% or more of the other side, or a stable deficit that the patient accepts (a modest deficit is expected without surgery [r3,r5])
Cuff strength about 90% or more of the other side, with no lag signs
No cramping or fatigue that limits heavy tasks
Completes progressive task- or sport-specific training without symptoms
After tenodesis: surgeon clearance, with attention to any concomitant cuff repair
tests: Hand-held dynamometry for elbow flexion, supination, external rotation and abduction compared with the other side
Repetition maximum or endurance test for row, curl and pull-up
External rotation lag sign and cuff strength at final assessment
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
QuickDASH or SPADI at baseline and return

prognosis: Most people do well without surgery. In one small old study, the conservative group lost 16% of elbow flexion strength and 11% of supination strength, compared with losses of 8% and 7% in the surgical group, and shoulder abduction strength fell by 16% and 20% [r5]. A review quotes a loss of 8–21% of flexion and supination power without surgery, and describes a small but evident gain after refixation [r3]. These are small, non-randomised and old data. The deformity persists without surgery, and some people have cramping; in the tenotomy-versus-tenodesis trials in painful but intact tendons, cosmetic deformity occurred in 33% after tenotomy and 10% after tenodesis at 24 months, without differences in pain or strength [r6], although the pooled data are indirect for acute rupture and many participants had a cuff repair at the same time [r13]. Long-term outcome is usually determined by the state of the cuff rather than by the biceps rupture [r3].
prevention: Treat persistent anterior shoulder pain and cuff weakness early, because a tendinopathic tendon is more likely to rupture (reasonable principle; not tested in the sources reviewed) [r4]
Avoid sudden heavy eccentric loading of the arm in people with known biceps or cuff tendinopathy (clinical reasoning)
Use a progressive strength program for the shoulder and arm, particularly in manual workers and lifters (reasonable principle)
Lift loads close to the body and avoid catching falling objects with the arm extended (clinical reasoning)
No intervention has been shown to prevent proximal biceps rupture in the sources reviewed here
clinicalPearls: A sudden pop and a Popeye bulge in someone with prior anterior shoulder pain is a long head rupture until proven otherwise. The shoulder often feels better afterwards, because the painful tendon is no longer loaded (clinical observation).

Always rule out a distal biceps rupture: about 3% of biceps ruptures [r1], with a much greater non-operative loss of supination (over 50%) and flexion (30–40%) power than a proximal rupture (8–21%), and operative treatment is the usual advice [r3].

Counsel with the numbers, and the limits of those numbers: roughly 8–21% loss of flexion and supination power [r3], 16% and 11% in the only measured conservative group [r5], from small, old, non-randomised data.
Residual shoulder pain after the rupture usually means the cuff, not the biceps: examine the cuff and subacromial space and image if weakness is more than expected [r3,r8].

Surgery is a priorities decision: younger, manual, sporting or cosmetic concerns favour tenodesis [r5,r3], but the best randomised data compare tenotomy and tenodesis in intact painful tendons and show no difference in pain, function or strength [r6,r11].
After tenodesis, protect the fixation: resisted active elbow flexion is delayed (commonly about 6 weeks), and a new deformity after a pop suggests failure.

animation.title: How a proximal biceps rupture happens

forces.label: Sudden load pulls the elbow straight

captions.text: A 60-year-old man with a sore front of the shoulder bends to pick up a heavy box.
He lifts it with his elbow bent, and the biceps tendon takes the load.
The load shifts suddenly, and the elbow is pulled straight against the contracting biceps.
A degenerate tendon cannot withstand the sudden pull, and there is a pop.
The arm still works, but the muscle belly starts to bunch up in the arm.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.

actions.text: Complete rupture of a degenerate tendon

captions.text: The long head of biceps runs through the joint and down the bicipital groove.
In many older people the tendon is already degenerate and weak.
A sudden heavy pull stretches the tendon beyond its capacity.
The fibres fail and the tendon ruptures, and the proximal end retracts.
The muscle still works through the short head, and its belly bunches toward the elbow.
Rotator cuff disease often coexists and can cause pain that continues after the rupture.
Tendon with aligned collagen; in older tendons the fibres are already thinner and less organised.
A sudden overload stretches the fibres past their limit.
The fibres rupture and the ends spring apart.
Blood leaks into the synovial space and tracks down the arm as bruising.
A synovial cap forms on each stump; the clot is diluted by joint fluid.
No bridging scar forms, so the stumps stay apart and the muscle remains retracted.
